h1:
Phatthalung Khanom Jeen
10 Shops for Fresh Noodles & Punchy Southern Curry
intro: If you ask a local for the one breakfast that really stands for Phatthalung, a lot of them will say khanom jeen with Southern curry — fresh rice noodles made every morning, ladled with punchy curries in several styles: jungle curry, coconut curry, gaeng tai pla and crab curry, eaten with a big pile of pak nao (fresh and blanched vegetables) you can refill as much as you like. Many of the well-known shops open from 5am and sell out before noon. We've picked the ones that are actually open right now, with the area, prices and hours.

blocks.html: Phatthalung's khanom jeen is a bit different from elsewhere because the town has been making fresh rice noodles for a long time. Many shops mill their own rice and press the noodles themselves every morning, so they come out softer, chewier and more fragrant than factory ones. The curries are proper Southern style — thick, hot, fragrant with turmeric and curry paste, and not sweet up front the way central-Thai versions can be. The other essential is pak nao: a big mound of fresh and blanched vegetables — yard-long beans, bean sprouts, cucumber, pennywort, sataw (stink beans), luk niang and cashew shoots — that you can keep refilling for free. It's the side that makes khanom jeen what it is.

blocks.text: How many curries does Phatthalung khanom jeen have, and how do you order?

blocks.html: Part of the fun of Phatthalung khanom jeen is that a single shop usually has several pots to choose from, and at some places you ladle it yourself. It helps to know the main curries before you go — ordering is a lot more fun once you do.

items: Nam ya gati (coconut curry) — pounded fish meat cooked with curry paste and coconut milk, pale orange, rounded and rich with a gentle heat. This is the one most first-timers like best.
Nam ya pa (jungle curry) — no coconut milk, punchy and hot with the full fragrance of the curry paste. For people who want it to land hard, and a good test of which shops make the real thing.

Gaeng tai pla — a thick, dark curry made from fermented fish innards, deeply savory and fragrant with spices, loaded with fish and vegetables. The strongest of all the curries here — if you eat Southern food well, you'll love it.
Green chicken curry — plenty of shops also serve green curry with chicken over the noodles, sweet and rich with mild heat. A good option for kids or anyone who doesn't want it fiery.
Crab curry (nam ya pu) — coconut curry with crab meat, rich and fragrant. It's a special order that costs a bit more than the regular curries, and some shops only have it on certain days.

blocks.title: How to eat it like a local
blocks.html: Locals like to spoon several curries onto one plate — say coconut curry mixed with jungle curry — then pile on the pak nao and toss it all together with a small squeeze of lime to cut the richness. Don't be shy about going back for a second round of pak nao; the shops mean it when they say refills are free.

blocks.text: 10 Phatthalung khanom jeen shops that are actually open

blocks.html: Ordered from the in-town shops that are easy for travelers to drop by, out to the neighborhood spots beyond town that Phatthalung locals drive to themselves. Most open early and sell out before noon, so plan to go early — that way you get the full range of curries and don't have to gamble on what's left.

items.name: Hua Khong Pak Phraek Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: The most famous khanom jeen shop in Phatthalung town, sitting on the bend of Pak Phraek Road. You grab a plate and ladle the curries yourself — Southern curry, coconut curry, gaeng tai pla, green chicken curry. The fresh noodles are the draw, along with hot fried chicken and fried pork straight from the wok. It opens from 5am, before sunrise, and there's a packed queue every morning — busy enough to have made the news.
items.meta: Pak Phraek Rd, Khuha Sawan, Mueang district · Daily 05:00–12:00

items.name: Nang Lat Khanom Jeen (the original)
items.blurb: One of Phatthalung's original khanom jeen shops — the owner, Pa Phorn, has developed her own curry recipes for more than 16 years. There are several curries to choose from: coconut curry, nam phrik, gaeng tai pla, green curry and jungle curry. Soft noodles, deep old-school curries, the kind of flavor locals point to as the real khanom jeen of the town.
items.meta: Soi Nang Lat 11, Khuha Sawan, Mueang district · Daily 08:00–14:00

items.name: Ban Thao Chan Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: A big, comfortable shop in the Chaiburi area, and a real community favorite — on weekends it's almost impossible to find a seat. Several curries to choose from, and the standout is the fried pork, crisp outside and tender inside, eaten alongside the noodles. Good for families or larger groups who want to sit down and take their time.

items.name: Na Rong Nom Jeen Phatthalung
items.blurb: A fresh-noodle shop in town with lots of reviews. The self-serve curries are 20 THB a bowl — Trang coconut curry, sour curry, jungle curry — while the special ones like gaeng tai pla, green chicken curry and crab curry are ladled for you at 30–40 THB. There's fried chicken and fried pork, plus local sweets like khanom duang to snack on. A good pick if you want to try several curries in one place.

items.name: Lang Juan Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: A neighborhood shop near Khlong Nui Bridge in town. The curries are punchy and properly hot in true Southern style, with fragrant herb-fried chicken on the side. Prices are easy, the way a local shop should be — good for anyone who wants the real heat with nothing toned down.
items.meta: Khlong Nui Bridge area, Mueang district · Morning–midday (check hours before you go)

items.name: Na Wat Phikun Thong Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: A khanom jeen shop in front of Wat Phikun Thong in the Khuan Khanun area. The curry is thick and punchy, with fried shrimp on the side, and it's where people around Khuan Khanun stop for breakfast before work. Handy if you're heading out to Thale Noi and want something to eat on the way.
items.meta: In front of Wat Phikun Thong, Khuan Khanun district · Daily 05:00–12:00

items.name: Pa Nit Khanom Jeen, Ban Sala Naen
items.blurb: A local shop in the Khuan Khanun area with punchy curries made fresh every morning. The noodles and curries are house-made, the kind of homey flavor people nearby eat regularly, at easy prices. Good if you want khanom jeen out of town that still tastes the old way.
items.meta: Ban Sala Naen, Khuan Khanun district · Daily 05:00–12:00

items.name: Na Sala Khanom Jeen, Ban Suan
items.blurb: A local shop in the Khuan Maphrao area. The curry is deep and traditional, with fragrant marinated grilled pork on the side — a homey place where locals eat as a matter of routine. Good if you want the atmosphere and flavor of a genuine village shop.
items.meta: Ban Suan, Khuan Maphrao, Mueang district · Daily 05:00–12:00

items.name: Phu Yai Sopha Khanom Jeen
items.blurb: A shop in the Phanang Tung area of Khuan Khanun. The curry is fiery and full of chili, with plenty of pak nao and pickled vegetables on the side. Good for anyone who likes proper Southern heat, and it's not far from Thale Noi, so you can stop in before or after the lotus-lake boat ride.
items.meta: Phanang Tung, Khuan Khanun district · Daily 05:00–12:00

items.name: Pa Yom Khanom Jeen, Highway 41
items.blurb: A roadside shop on Highway 41 in the Khuan Khanun area, with both spicy curry and coconut curry made with fish — and on some days boiled duck eggs to eat alongside. Easy parking, so it's good for anyone driving through who wants to stop for an early-morning bowl of khanom jeen before carrying on.
items.meta: Roadside on Highway 41, Khuan Khanun district · Daily 05:00–12:00

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: The famous in-town shops like Hua Khong Pak Phraek get long lines between 7 and 9am. If you'd rather not wait, go before 7, or skip out to the neighborhood shops around Khuan Khanun that are just as good and far less crowded. Crab curry is a special order — some shops don't have it every day and it sells out fast, so if you want it, call ahead or get there early.

blocks.text: Planning a half-morning khanom jeen crawl in Phatthalung

blocks.html: Khanom jeen is a breakfast thing, and the bowls are small, so you can hit a few shops in one morning. Try a morning like this — get up a little early and you'll catch both the famous in-town shop and a local one, then carry on to Thale Noi later in the morning.

items.activity: Start at Hua Khong Pak Phraek
items.note: Go before the line gets long, ladle your own curries, try coconut curry + gaeng tai pla, and order the fried chicken hot from the wok

items.activity: On to Nang Lat for the jungle curry
items.note: Opens right at 8 — try the punchy 16-year-recipe jungle curry and compare it with the first shop

items.activity: Grab a second round of pak nao
items.note: If you've still got room, pile on more pak nao tossed with the curry and a squeeze of lime to cut the richness before you head off

items.activity: Drive out to Khuan Khanun, stop at the Wat Phikun Thong shop
items.note: Thick curry with fried shrimp — breakfast before heading to Thale Noi

items.activity: Boat ride to see the red lotuses at Thale Noi
items.note: The lotuses are at their best in the morning, with lots of birds and the air still cool

items.activity: Stop at Pa Yom on Highway 41 on the way back
items.note: If you're still hungry, try the fish coconut curry — easy parking, a fitting end to the khanom jeen trip

faq.q: Which khanom jeen shop in Phatthalung is the most famous?
faq.a: Hua Khong Pak Phraek is the most famous in Phatthalung town, sitting on the bend of Pak Phraek Road. It opens from 5am, you ladle several curries yourself, and there's a packed queue every morning. Nang Lat is the old original, an heirloom recipe that locals point to as the real khanom jeen of the town.

faq.q: What time does Phatthalung khanom jeen open, and does it sell out fast?
faq.a: Most shops are a breakfast thing, open from 5am to noon. Some, like Nang Lat, open from 8am to 2pm. The famous shops usually sell out before noon, so it's best to go between 6 and 9am to get the full range of curries and the freshest noodles.

faq.q: About how much does Phatthalung khanom jeen cost?
faq.a: Regular self-serve curries start at 20 THB a bowl. The special ones that get ladled for you, like gaeng tai pla or green chicken curry, are around 30 THB, and crab curry is around 40 THB. A real meal usually comes to under 100 THB per person. Pak nao refills are unlimited at no extra charge.

faq.q: What is pak nao, and how do you eat it with khanom jeen?
faq.a: Pak nao is the fresh and blanched vegetables that Southern Thailand serves alongside khanom jeen — yard-long beans, bean sprouts, cucumber, pennywort, sataw (stink beans), luk niang and cashew shoots — refilled as much as you like. You toss it together with the noodles and curry to cut the heat and add fresh crunch. It's an essential part of Southern khanom jeen.

faq.q: Is Phatthalung khanom jeen very spicy? Can kids eat it?
faq.a: Jungle curry and gaeng tai pla are fiery in true Southern style, while the coconut curry is more rounded and less spicy — good for first-timers. If you're bringing kids, many shops have green chicken curry over the noodles, which is sweet and rich with mild heat, an easy option for them.
